title: French Revolution: People and Factions
subtitle: Trace how ideas, alliances, and conflict reshaped France
overview: Explore a focused network of thinkers, rulers, reformers, and revolutionaries to see how relationships and political choices changed the direction of the French Revolution.
essentialQuestion: How did relationships and competing ideas change the course of the French Revolution?

objectives.title: Identify major roles
objectives.description: Recognize key people and the political or social roles they played.

objectives.title: Compare political positions
objectives.description: Distinguish reformers, radicals, monarchists, and later leaders.

objectives.title: Trace influence and conflict
objectives.description: Follow a chain from Enlightenment ideas to revolutionary action.

objectives.title: Explain cause and effect
objectives.description: Use evidence to explain how a changing relationship affected events.

groups.name: Monarchy
groups.description: The royal household and defenders of inherited authority.

groups.name: Constitutional Reform
groups.description: People seeking political change with constitutional limits.

groups.name: Radical Revolution
groups.description: Leaders associated with popular mobilization and radical republican politics.

groups.name: Ideas and Rights
groups.description: Thinkers and advocates whose writing shaped political arguments.

groups.name: Post-Revolution Power
groups.description: Leadership that emerged from the Revolution's later instability.

characters.name: Louis XVI
characters.summary: Louis XVI faced a financial and political crisis and struggled to preserve royal authority as demands for representation grew.

characters.name: Marie Antoinette
characters.summary: Marie Antoinette became a powerful public symbol in revolutionary criticism, although many claims about her were exaggerated or false.

characters.name: Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette
characters.summary: Lafayette supported a constitutional monarchy and commanded the National Guard, placing him between royal authority and popular revolution.

characters.name: Maximilien Robespierre
characters.summary: Robespierre argued for republican virtue and became a leading figure in the Committee of Public Safety during the Revolution's radical phase.

characters.name: Georges Danton
characters.summary: Danton helped mobilize revolutionary politics and later called for restraint, bringing him into conflict with former allies.

characters.name: Jean-Paul Marat
characters.summary: Marat used journalism to demand stronger revolutionary action and became closely associated with popular radicalism.

characters.name: Olympe de Gouges
characters.summary: Olympe de Gouges demanded political rights for women and criticized violence and exclusion within the Revolution.

characters.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
characters.summary: Rousseau wrote about popular sovereignty and the general will, ideas later interpreted in different ways by revolutionaries.

characters.name: Napoleon Bonaparte
characters.summary: Napoleon rose through the revolutionary army and later concentrated power, carrying some revolutionary reforms while ending republican government.

relationships.summary: Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette were the royal couple.
relationships.evidenceSummary: Their marriage joined the French and Habsburg dynasties and made both central symbols of the monarchy.

relationships.summary: Lafayette tried to protect a constitutional monarchy.
relationships.evidenceSummary: As National Guard commander, Lafayette guarded the royal family while also supporting constitutional limits on the king.

relationships.summary: Lafayette and Robespierre favored different directions for the Revolution.
relationships.evidenceSummary: Lafayette defended constitutional monarchy while Robespierre increasingly argued for republican and radical democratic positions.

relationships.summary: Robespierre drew on ideas associated with Rousseau.
relationships.evidenceSummary: Robespierre repeatedly used ideas of popular sovereignty, virtue, and the general will associated with Rousseau's political writing.

relationships.summary: Olympe de Gouges engaged with Enlightenment arguments about citizenship.
relationships.evidenceSummary: Her rights writing answered a political culture shaped by social-contract ideas while challenging its exclusion of women.
relationships.disputeNote: Historians differ on how directly Rousseau's writing influenced de Gouges; the link is presented as intellectual context, not proven personal mentorship.

relationships.evidenceSummary: Robespierre argued that the king's position threatened the republic and supported a political break with monarchy.

relationships.summary: Former revolutionary allies became political rivals.
relationships.evidenceSummary: Danton's calls for reducing repression conflicted with the Committee of Public Safety; he was tried and executed in April 1794.

relationships.summary: Robespierre and Marat shared important radical causes.
relationships.evidenceSummary: Both opposed the Girondins and supported stronger popular and republican action, although they were not identical in methods or goals.

relationships.summary: Danton and Marat operated in overlapping radical circles.
relationships.evidenceSummary: Both were associated with the Cordeliers milieu and popular pressure for a republic, even when their tactics differed.

relationships.summary: De Gouges criticized radical political violence and concentration of power.
relationships.evidenceSummary: Her political writings defended inclusive rights and criticized revolutionary extremism before her arrest and execution in 1793.

relationships.summary: The queen distrusted Lafayette's constitutional reform role.
relationships.evidenceSummary: Lafayette's attempt to balance monarchy and revolution made him unacceptable to committed royalists as well as radicals.

relationships.summary: The Revolution's radical institutions shaped the world in which Napoleon rose.
relationships.evidenceSummary: Napoleon benefited from military and political openings created by the Revolution, but a direct personal ideological line from Robespierre is not established.
relationships.disputeNote: This edge represents institutional and historical context rather than a proven direct personal influence.

missions.title: Find the Jacobin leader
missions.prompt: Select the character who became a leading figure in the Committee of Public Safety.
hints: Look inside the Radical Revolution group.

missions.title: Map the radical network
missions.prompt: Select the three revolutionary leaders grouped with radical republican politics.
hints: Robespierre is one of the three; look for a journalist and a powerful speaker.

missions.title: Trace an idea into conflict
missions.prompt: Trace a path from Rousseau's political ideas through Robespierre to conflict with Louis XVI.
hints: Start with an influence edge, then follow the strongest conflict with monarchy.

missions.title: Compare two directions
missions.prompt: Compare Lafayette's constitutional approach with Robespierre's republican position using their roles and relationships.
hints: Ask what each person believed should happen to royal authority.

missions.title: Explain a broken alliance
missions.prompt: Explain how the conflict between Danton and Robespierre shows a change inside the Revolution.
hints: Review why Danton began calling for restraint.

discussionQuestions: When does political compromise protect a revolution, and when might it weaken one?
How should we distinguish a person's real actions from the public image created around them?

preparedAssessment.prompt: Which person most clearly represented constitutional monarchy in this lesson?
Which relationship connects Enlightenment political ideas to radical revolutionary leadership?
Why did Danton and Robespierre become rivals?
options: Danton called for restraint while Robespierre's committee continued repression

preparedAssessment.prompt: Compare one reformer and one radical using evidence from the galaxy.
Which relationship in this lesson best explains why revolutions can change direction?

preparedSummary: You explored how political ideas moved through relationships instead of acting on events by themselves.
You compared constitutional reform with radical republican change.
You used a broken alliance to explain how the Revolution changed from within.
